messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Javier, a 40-year-old married surgeon of Latin American descent, sought help after months of escalating distress following a devastating earthquake that struck his hometown two years prior. He had been on duty in the hospital when the earth violently convulsed, bringing down parts of the old building and igniting fires in the shattered infrastructure. The cacophony of crumbling concrete, piercing screams, and the acrid smell of burning insulation and flesh remained seared into his mind. He spent days operating under makeshift conditions, surrounded by the overwhelming smells of smoke and burnt debris, witnessing unimaginable suffering.

Now, ordinary life had become a minefield. Javier found that even the most innocuous sensory cues could instantly plunge him back into the horror. A sudden, loud noise, like a car backfiring on the street outside his suburban home, or the sharp clang of surgical instruments dropping in the operating room, could without warning bring back the full, terrifying memory of the earthquake. Similarly, the faint smell of smoke from a neighbor’s barbecue, or the distinct burnt smell of cauterized tissue during surgery, would instantly transport him, his heart pounding, to the chaos of those days. These potent triggers were not just fleeting reminders; they were gateways to vivid, visceral flashbacks that felt terrifyingly real.

What complicated Javier’s internal world was the peculiar nature of these recollections. When a trigger would strike, he would be overwhelmed by the memory, yet he felt like he was only remembering parts of what happened, with the rest frustratingly missing or blurred. This incomplete picture of the event, coupled with the overwhelming grief that consumed him every time he recalled the trauma, left him in a constant state of internal agitation. This persistent internal turmoil, fueled by the fragmented and deeply sorrowful memories, made him acutely sensitive to his surroundings. He found himself hyper-vigilant, scanning for any potential threat, and this heightened state of awareness meant that more and more everyday sounds and smells began to register as danger cues, effectively generating new triggers and reinforcing the cycle of distress.

To cope with this relentless onslaught, Javier had developed several maladaptive strategies. After a particularly demanding day in the operating room, where the smells and sounds were often too close for comfort, he would retreat into himself. He would distract himself by immersing himself in complex medical journals or binge-watching television shows for hours. More often than not, he would pour himself a generous glass of whiskey, sometimes two, finding temporary solace in the numbing effect of the alcohol. He also found a release for his tension in sexual fantasies and activities, using them as an escape from the anxiety that coiled in his gut. While these strategies offered immediate, albeit fleeting, relief from the overwhelming distress that followed the triggers and subsequent memory intrusions, they came at a cost. By consistently distracting himself, drinking, or seeking sexual release instead of allowing himself to process the traumatic experience, he inadvertently prevented the memory from integrating into a coherent narrative. This avoidance meant the memory remained fragmented, an incomplete picture of terror and loss, thereby sustaining the raw, overwhelming grief he felt each time it surfaced.

The cumulative effect of these cycles had begun to take a toll on Javier’s professional life. His distraction made it harder to focus during long surgeries, and his reliance on alcohol meant he often felt sluggish and irritable at home. He had come to believe that the world was still a dangerous place, and that he was fundamentally flawed for not being able to "get over it." He sought help feeling exhausted and increasingly isolated, desperately hoping to find a way to quiet the constant internal alarms and piece together the fragmented story of his trauma.
